dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the ISA, simulator, and reference kernel

evidence.note: Read all of problem.py in three passes (ISA, slot limits, VLEN, execution loop, reference kernels, hash stages) plus run_tests.sh and submission_tests.py before editing — thorough enumeration of the machine model up front.
First SIMD rewrite passed correctness immediately, showing the numeric contract / computation to reproduce was decoded correctly.
Recognized hash-stage shift-left equals multiplication and fused into multiply_add — precise grasp of hash-stage data dependencies and op semantics.
Distinguished load slots, flow/vselect engine, and vector ALU as separate resource classes and balanced ops across them — evidence of an accurate per-slot cost model.
Quantitative scratch-memory constraints cited (1472 / 1536 words) to size register sets — treating source limits as ground truth.
Nearly all later reads were of kernel.py rather than problem.py; orientation was front-loaded with little mid-optimization return to source to resolve new ambiguities, short of the level-10 behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent fully read problem.py, the tests, and the reference kernel before acting, enumerating ISA/slots/VLEN, correctly restating the computation (first-try correctness), understanding hash-stage semantics (shift=multiply), distinguishing load/flow/ALU engines, and reasoning quantitatively about scratch limits and the scarce resource — matching the level-8 'precise model with op-class costs, hash dependencies, and numeric contract' anchor. It falls short of level 10 because orientation was largely front-loaded and it seldom revisited problem.py to resolve ambiguities mid-optimization; the summary-only log also limits certainty, hence medium confidence.

dimensions.name: Staging the 118x speedup into checkpoints

evidence.note: Establishes baseline (147,734 cycles) then replaces scalar with SIMD and explicitly confirms correctness first — a correct-rewrite checkpoint before optimizing.
Explicit phase boundary: 'transition to the scheduling and instruction packing phase' — shows ordered phasing (correct → vectorize → pack).
Sequential distinct optimization phases (list-scheduling, register decoupling T=8/20/28, multiply_add strength reduction), each followed by a test run — phases worked roughly in order and measured.

Tries 28-set config, finds it worse, reverts and 'writes back the 20-sets configuration to lock in our absolute best result of 1814' — preserving a known-good best / fallback behavior characteristic of higher anchors.

Later phases (wrap-around, load prioritization, register maximization) chosen against observed bottlenecks, but framed as one-off optimizations rather than gated numeric milestones; no explicit '<20k/<5k/<1250' ladder defined upfront.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly identified and worked ordered phases (correct SIMD baseline → VLIW packing/scheduling → register decoupling → strength reduction → global pipelining), measuring after each and reverting to a preserved best when a change regressed — matching anchor 5 with some anchor-8 traits (known-good preservation). However it never established an explicit quantitative milestone ladder with pre-set cycle gates; intermediate targets appeared reactively ('below 1500', 'close to 1000'). This places it between anchors 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Correctness + cycle verification beyond run_tests.sh

evidence.note: Runs run_tests.sh after essentially every meaningful kernel change, checking both correctness and cycle count before proceeding — solid anchor-5 loop discipline.
Builds a custom diagnostic script (test_schedule.py) to measure per-round scheduled bundle counts and test 16-set configs before applying — tighter cycle feedback than run_tests.sh provides.
Uses the custom harness to compare register-set configurations (16/20/28) and scheduler priority keys, doing per-configuration cycle attribution prior to committing changes into kernel.py.
Fixes RecursionError in dependency builder — reactive correctness fix, but caught via testing rather than an independent correctness harness.

Reasons about mathematical correctness of omitting wrap-around checks, but never builds differential testing vs the reference on custom inputs nor verifies slot-limit legality independently — correctness verification stays reliant on run_tests.sh.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor-5: it runs run_tests.sh after every meaningful change (checking correctness and cycles) AND builds a custom diagnostic harness for per-round cycle measurement and configuration comparison — feedback beyond the provided tool. However it falls short of anchor-8 because that extra harness targets cycles/scheduling only; correctness is never independently verified via differential testing on custom inputs, sub-computation isolation, or independent slot-limit legality checks, remaining dependent on the single provided test's green run. This mix of strong cycle verification and standard correctness verification places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking cycles-to-target and detecting plateaus

evidence.note: Built repeated diagnostics to measure per-round scheduled bundle counts, showing active tracking of where cycles are spent rather than just a single final number.

Compared T=16/20/28 register-set configurations, tied predicted cycle deltas to specific changes (e.g. '144 to 134'), and iterated on which config lowers cycles — but many numbers are predictions, not confirmed measurements.
Tested 20-set vs 28-set configs, found 28 worse, and reverted to 20-sets as 'absolute best' — attributing deltas and pivoting off an unproductive line rather than grinding.
Locked in 1814 cycles and declared '81.4x speedup' success despite the 1250 target being unmet — an inaccurate picture of distance-to-target at the close, capping the level.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently tracked cycle counts across iterations, knew it was aiming at 1250, used diagnostics to find bottlenecks, and attributed deltas to specific config changes while reverting to the best-measured option (above the level-5 anchor, touching the level-8 behavior of attributing deltas and pivoting). But it frequently conflated predicted with measured gains and, decisively, terminated at 1814 cycles while framing it as success — a failure to keep an accurate running picture of distance to the 1250 target — which keeps it short of the sustained, target-honest monitoring at 8. This places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when a transformation fails or backfires

evidence.note: Diagnosed the RecursionError's root cause (self-loops where reader==node_id break the DAG assumption) and fixed the dependency builder — a genuine root-cause correction rather than a random tweak.
When list-scheduling density was limited, reasoned about WAW/WAR artificial dependencies and adjusted the register-set model (T=8→20, then decoupled 8/16 sets) — measurement-informed model update.
Profiled load density per cycle in Round 3 to diagnose why loads weren't packed to 100%, steering scheduler priority changes — diagnosing which resource assumption was wrong.
Compared 20-set vs 28-set configs and reverted to 20-set as the best (1814), preserving the known-good baseline instead of barrelling ahead — revert-and-retry informed by the result.

Declared 1814 cycles a success despite the <1250 target being missed; no decisive abandonment of the single list-scheduling strategy nor re-derivation of the milestone ladder from the shortfall — falls short of the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows solid mid-level adaptation: it diagnoses concrete divergences at the root (the RecursionError self-loop, sub-100% load density) and reverts to the known-good register configuration when a variant (28-sets) fails to help, matching anchors 5 and touching 8 for specific instances. However, the overall arc stays within one strategy tuned by empirical parameter sweeps rather than decisive strategy pivots, and it never treats the missed 1250 target as evidence requiring re-derivation of the plan, so it does not reach the 8–10 band. Confidence is medium because the trajectory is prose-only intentions with a large hidden gap (steps 213→428).

dimensions.name: Quantitative bottleneck / lower-bound reasoning

evidence.note: Quantitative op-class reduction: reasons that shift-left = multiply, cutting hash vector-ALU ops from 18 to 12, targeting the dominant op class.
Identifies load slots as the binding resource ('fill the load slots perfectly', investigates 'why loads are not packed to 100% density'), directing scheduling effort at the scarce port.
Reasons about register-set count reducing load-start delay to cut round cost '144 to 134', an empirical-plus-structural estimate of bundle need per round.
Computes savings of '960 vector ALU instructions' by dropping wrap-around checks, showing work-volume accounting to pick targets.

Names 'bottleneck on the vector ALU' when choosing register config, but ends by declaring 1814 the 'absolute best' with no lower-bound comparison to the 1250 target—no roofline judgment of remaining headroom.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently counts op classes and identifies which resource (load slots, vector ALU, register pressure) bounds each phase, and uses that to pick targets—clearly above anchor 5. However it never computes a defensible cycle lower bound from work volume and slot width, and closes without a roofline assessment of whether further gains were possible (it stalled at 1814 vs. 1250 and simply called it best), so it does not reach anchor 8. This places the observed level at 6.

rubric.task_read: An extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task: reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA + simulator (problem.py, SLOT_LIMITS, HASH_STAGES, reference kernel) and rewrite /app/kernel.py to run a ~118x faster (147,734 → <1250 cycles) kernel that stays correct on randomized inputs. Difficulty comes from (a) deep understanding of an unfamiliar machine model and the reference semantics, and (b) sustained, quantitatively-driven optimization — vectorization, bundle/slot packing, scheduling — where naive effort plateaus far short of the target. This warrants heavy, sustained meta-work across all five faculties.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the ISA, simulator, and reference kernel
dimensions.description: Reading problem.py to build an accurate model of the machine — ISA/opcodes, per-slot limits, hash stages, cycle-cost model — and inferring exactly what the reference kernel must compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The entire optimization space, correctness contract, and cost model are latent in problem.py; every downstream decision (which ops are cheap, how many slots per bundle, what result must match) depends on how accurately the agent decodes the environment before and while optimizing.

anchors.0: Edits kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at the ISA.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; grasps a few opcodes but misunderstands slot limits, the cost model, or what the kernel must output.
anchors.5: Reads the simulator and reference kernel enough to enumerate available ops, understand the per-cycle/per-slot cost model, and correctly restate the computation to be reproduced.
anchors.8: Builds a precise mental (or written) model: exact SLOT_LIMITS per unit, cost of each op class, data dependencies of the hash stages, and the numeric contract the output must satisfy — and cites specific lines/behaviors to justify it.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete quantitative machine model (what a bundle can issue per cycle, which resource is scarcest, where the reference wastes cycles) and revisits problem.py to resolve specific ambiguities as they arise mid-optimization, treating the source as ground truth rather than assumption.

dimensions.name: Staging the 118x speedup into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the huge gap into an ordered ladder — e.g. correct rewrite → vectorized → slot-packed/scheduled → target — each with a concrete cycle/correctness checkpoint, rather than one undifferentiated optimization push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A ~118x reduction is unreachable in one leap; without intermediate targets and a known-good baseline to fall back to, the agent cannot tell which transformation bought which savings or recover from a regression.

anchors.0: No sub-goals; blindly tweaks the kernel hoping the number drops.
anchors.3: Vague ordering ('make it faster') with no explicit intermediate targets or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies a few phases (get correct first, then vectorize, then pack) and works them roughly in order.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit milestone ladder with quantitative gates (e.g. 'correct baseline', '<20k', '<5k', '<1250') and a preserved known-good version at each rung.
anchors.10: Milestones are derived from the cost model (each targets a specific bottleneck with an estimated cycle payoff), sequenced by dependency and expected ROI, and revised as measurements reveal where the real cycles are.

dimensions.name: Correctness + cycle verification beyond run_tests.sh
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that catch both correctness regressions (across randomized inputs) and cycle changes, rather than trusting a single final test run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Aggressive SIMD/packing transformations silently break correctness or violate slot limits; a tight, frequent verification loop is what separates real progress from a fast-but-wrong kernel.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only at the very end; no correctness checking during changes.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a green run as sufficient and does no independent correctness reasoning.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after meaningful changes and checks both correctness and the cycle count before proceeding.
anchors.8: Builds tighter feedback than provided: diffs against the reference on custom/edge inputs, isolates sub-computations, and verifies slot-limit legality of bundles independently before the full test.
anchors.10: Maintains a layered verification harness — fast unit checks on individual stages, randomized differential testing vs. the reference, and per-transformation cycle attribution — so any regression is caught and localized immediately rather than discovered at the end.

dimensions.name: Tracking cycles-to-target and detecting plateaus
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate running picture of current cycle count vs. the 1250 target and whether recent edits are still yielding gains or thrashing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization horizon it is easy to burn effort on transformations that don't move the number; recognizing a plateau or a regression early is what prevents wasted cycles of engineering.

anchors.0: Loses track of the current cycle count or whether changes helped; no sense of distance to target.
anchors.3: Knows the latest number but not the trend; repeats ineffective tweaks without noticing.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across iterations and knows roughly how far from 1250, adjusting effort accordingly.
anchors.8: Attributes cycle deltas to specific changes, notices when a line of attack has stopped paying off, and pivots rather than grinding on it.
anchors.10: Sustains a quantitative ledger of where cycles are spent vs. the theoretical floor, continuously reprioritizing toward the largest remaining bottleneck and explicitly recognizing diminishing returns or circular re-tuning.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when a transformation fails or backfires
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization or scheduling strategy when measurements contradict expectations (a packing breaks slot limits, a rewrite regresses cycles, an assumed op is expensive).
dimensions.why_it_matters: The cost model has surprises; barrelling ahead on a falsified assumption (e.g. a bundle that can't legally issue, or a 'vectorization' that costs more) wastes the long horizon and can strand the kernel in a broken state.

anchors.0: Repeats the same failing approach; ignores contradicting test results.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with random tweaks rather than diagnosing why the assumption was wrong.
anchors.5: When a change regresses or breaks, reverts and tries a different tactic informed by the failure.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the root cause of a divergence (which slot/cost assumption was wrong), updates the machine model, and redirects the plan accordingly.
anchors.10: Treats surprises as evidence that refines the cost model, abandons whole strategies decisively when the data warrants, and re-derives the milestone ladder from the corrected understanding — without losing the known-good baseline.

dimensions.name: Quantitative bottleneck / lower-bound reasoning
dimensions.description: Reasoning explicitly about the theoretical cycle floor and which hardware resource (slots, ports, dependency chains) bounds performance, to steer optimization toward what actually matters.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x target is only reachable by targeting the binding constraint; roofline-style reasoning about the minimum bundles needed and the scarcest slot distinguishes principled optimization from trial-and-error tweaking.

anchors.0: No reasoning about limits; purely empirical poking.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy 'this should be faster' with no quantitative basis.
anchors.5: Estimates roughly how many bundles the work needs and which op class dominates, using that to pick targets.
anchors.8: Computes a defensible lower bound on cycles from the work volume and slot limits, and directs effort at the resource that bound identifies.
anchors.10: Maintains a sharp roofline-style model (min bundles given SIMD width, slot ports, and dependency latency), uses it to judge how close to optimal the kernel is, and knows when further effort is futile vs. when headroom remains.
